walkthroughs.title: Immutable Scala collections: filter, partition, map and fold without losing data

steps.title: filter keeps rows, partition keeps both sides
steps.explanation: object Main is a singleton that holds the program's functions; the JVM starts at its main method. Seq is an immutable sequence, so filter and partition never change the input; they return new sequences. The underscore in _ >= 0L is shorthand for 'each element'. filter keeps only amounts that are zero or more, while partition returns a pair: the matching amounts and the rejected ones. Keeping the rejected side is what lets a pipeline explain every input row later.
steps.observe: Order and duplicates are preserved; filter does not deduplicate.

steps.title: A guarded map and a fold that carries two values
steps.explanation: require throws IllegalArgumentException when its condition is false, so fivePercent refuses negative amounts before doing any work. Dividing by 20 gives five percent rounded down without multiplying first, which could overflow a Long. foldLeft walks the sequence from left to right with an accumulator, here a tuple of (count, total). Math.addExact throws ArithmeticException on overflow instead of silently wrapping around.
steps.observe: summary of an empty sequence returns its starting value (0, 0), which is the correct identity.

steps.title: Counting occurrences and summarizing per group
steps.explanation: frequencies builds an immutable Map by folding: updated returns a new map with one key changed, and getOrElse supplies 0 for a key seen for the first time. groupedSummary first rejects blank group labels, then filters out negative amounts, groups rows by label with groupBy, and reuses summary for each group. Validating labels before filtering matters: otherwise a bad label on a negative row would be filtered away and never reported.
steps.observe: A group whose rows are all negative disappears from the report, by design.

steps.title: Helpers that expect a failure
steps.explanation: body: => Any is a by-name parameter: the argument expression is not evaluated when the helper is called but each time body is used inside it. That lets the helper run the risky expression inside its own try block. If the expected exception is caught, the flag is set; assert then fails the program if no exception happened.
steps.observe: These helpers turn 'this call must fail' into a check that passes.

steps.excerpt:
def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    // Exercise 1: Retain observed zero and repeated values
    val raw = Seq(100L, -5L, 0L, 100L, 25L)
    assert(accepted(raw) == Seq(100L, 0L, 100L, 25L))
    assert(raw == Seq(100L, -5L, 0L, 100L, 25L))
    assert(accepted(Seq.empty[Long]).isEmpty)
    // Exercise 2: Keep a rejected ledger
    val split = partitionAmounts(raw)
    assert(split._1 == Seq(100L, 0L, 100L, 25L) && split._2 == Seq(-5L))
    assert(split._1.size + split._2.size == raw.size)
    assert(partitionAmounts(Seq(-2L, -1L)) == (Seq.empty[Long], Seq(-2L, -1L)))
    // Exercise 3: Map a bounded numeric policy
    assert(fivePercent(accepted(raw)) == Seq(5L, 0L, 5L, 1L))
    assert(fivePercent(Seq(Long.MaxValue)) == Seq(Long.MaxValue / 20L))
    expectIllegalArgument(fivePercent(Seq(-1L)))
steps.title: Checks for filtering, partitioning and fees
steps.explanation: The fixture has 100, -5, 0, 100 and 25 cents. Accepting nonnegative values keeps four entries, including both 100s and the zero. The partition check adds the sizes back up to five so nothing is lost. The fee for 25 cents is 1 because integer division rounds down. Long.MaxValue / 20 shows the overflow-safe order of operations.
steps.observe: The fees are 5, 0, 5 and 1, and a negative amount is rejected.

steps.title: Totals, frequencies, grouped report and the result lines
steps.explanation: The accepted values count 4 and total 225. Adding 1 to Long.MaxValue is rejected by addExact. The frequency map compares equal regardless of key order because Map equality is by content. The grouped report reconciles back to the same count and total. Then the program prints a success line followed by a version line; the version line depends on the installed Scala and Java, so only the first line is a stable expected output.
steps.observe: The first printed line is: spark-004: six reference contracts passed

walkthroughs.title: PySpark window functions: deterministic winners, running totals and lag
expected_output: spark-019: six PySpark reference contracts passed; Spark=4.3.0

steps.title: Validate identities, then rank with a full tie breaker
steps.explanation: validate_candidates computes the row count and the distinct event_id count in one aggregation and rejects the data if they differ, or if any id is not positive or entity is missing. rank_candidates defines a window: partitionBy splits rows per entity, and orderBy sorts newest event_time first with missing times last, then by event_id descending. row_number gives 1, 2, 3 within each entity. Because event_id is unique, the order is total and rank 1 is always the same row.
steps.observe: winners keeps exactly one row per entity and drops the helper rank column.

steps.title: Why ordering by time alone is not enough
steps.explanation: top_time_candidates orders only by event_time and uses dense_rank, which gives tied rows the same rank. When two events share the latest timestamp, both get rank 1. Using row_number with this incomplete ordering would silently pick one of them, and which one could change with partitioning. This function exposes the tie instead of hiding it.
steps.observe: Entities with tied latest times return more than one candidate.

steps.title: ROWS versus RANGE frames, and lag
steps.explanation: A window frame says which rows feed each calculation. rowsBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow) sums physical rows up to this one, so tied timestamps get different running totals. rangeBetween uses the ordering value instead, so all rows with the same time are peers and share one total. lag reads the previous row's value in the same ordered partition; the first row of each entity gets null. Subtracting unix timestamps gives the gap in seconds.
steps.observe: Tied rows 2 and 3 have rows totals 30 and 60 but the same peer total 60.

def main():
    spark = (
        SparkSession.builder.appName("ds60-spark-019")
        .master("local[2]")
        .config("spark.ui.enabled", "false")
        .config("spark.driver.host", "127.0.0.1")
        .config("spark.driver.bindAddress", "127.0.0.1")
        .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "2")
        .config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false")
        .config("spark.sql.ansi.enabled", "true")
        .config("spark.sql.session.timeZone", "UTC")
        .getOrCreate()
    )
    try:
        assert spark.sparkContext.master == "local[2]"
        spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR")
        schema = StructType(
            [
                StructField("event_id", LongType(), False),
                StructField("entity", StringType(), False),
                StructField("time_text", StringType(), True),
                StructField("amount", LongType(), False),
            ]
        )
        events = spark.createDataFrame(
            [
                (1, "A", "2024-01-01 00:00:00", 10),
                (2, "A", "2024-01-01 00:01:00", 20),
                (3, "A", "2024-01-01 00:01:00", 30),
                (4, "B", "2024-01-01 00:00:00", 40),
                (5, "B", "2024-01-01 00:02:00", 50),
                (6, "B", "2024-01-01 00:02:00", 60),
                (7, "C", None, 70),
                (8, "C", "2024-01-01 00:01:00", 80),
            ],
            schema=schema,
        ).withColumn("event_time", F.to_timestamp("time_text"))
steps.title: A local session and a small typed DataFrame
steps.explanation: The builder creates a SparkSession on local[2], meaning two worker threads in this one process, with the web UI off and the driver bound to localhost so nothing listens on the network. Fixing shuffle partitions, disabling adaptive execution, enabling ANSI mode and setting the time zone to UTC make results repeatable. The explicit StructType schema states each column's type and nullability. to_timestamp then parses the time text, and the None for event 7 becomes a null timestamp.
steps.observe: events has eight rows across entities A, B and C.

steps.title: Rejecting duplicates and checking winners across layouts
steps.explanation: Unioning a second copy of event 1 must make validation raise ValueError; the try, except, else pattern turns 'no error' into an AssertionError. The rank table is checked row by row. Winners are then recomputed after repartitioning to 1, 3 and 4 partitions, which shuffles the physical layout. Because the ordering is total, the winners stay 3, 6 and 8 every time. The same logic written in Spark SQL returns the same ids.
steps.observe: The winners are 3, 6 and 8 in every layout and in SQL.

steps.title: Ties, frame totals, lag rows and the result line
steps.explanation: The incomplete ordering returns five candidates, and entities A and B each have two. The running total table shows the ROWS and RANGE difference, and event 7 with a missing time sorts last in entity C. In the lag table, event 7's previous id is 8 but its gap is null, because one side of the subtraction is unknown. The finally block always stops the session, even after a failure. Collects are tiny and sorted before comparison.
steps.observe: The program prints: spark-019: six PySpark reference contracts passed; Spark=4.3.0

walkthroughs.title: Structured Streaming checkpoints: resume, empty resume and separate replay
expected_output: spark-035: six Scala reference contracts passed; Spark=4.3.0

steps.title: A fixed schema, owned scratch and atomic file publication
steps.explanation: eventSchema declares the two Long columns every input file must have, so Spark never has to guess types. deleteOwned only deletes a directory whose name starts with spark- directly under the working directory, a guard against deleting the wrong path. publishFile writes the JSON lines to a pending file first and then moves it into the input folder with ATOMIC_MOVE. A streaming file source could otherwise see a half-written file.
steps.observe: Input files appear in the input folder only when they are complete.

steps.excerpt:
def runParquet(spark: SparkSession, input: Path, checkpoint: Path, output: Path): RunReceipt = {
    val source = spark.readStream
      .schema(eventSchema)
      .option("maxFilesPerTrigger", 1)
      .option("mode", "FAILFAST")
      .json(input.toString)
    val query = source.writeStream
      .format("parquet")
      .outputMode("append")
      .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint.toString)
      .trigger(Trigger.AvailableNow())
      .start(output.toString)
    ownedQueries += query
    try {
      require(query.awaitTermination(45000L), "Finite query exceeded 45-second deadline")
      require(query.exception.isEmpty, "Finite query failed")
      RunReceipt(
        query.id.toString,
        query.runId.toString,
        query.recentProgress.map(_.numInputRows).sum,
        query.recentProgress.map(_.batchId).toSeq
      )
    } finally { if (query.isActive) query.stop() }
  }
steps.title: One finite streaming run
steps.explanation: readStream treats the input folder as a stream and reads one file per micro batch. FAILFAST makes malformed JSON an error instead of a silent null row. writeStream appends to Parquet and records its progress in checkpointLocation. Trigger.AvailableNow processes everything available right now and then stops, which makes a streaming query finite and testable. The receipt records the query id, the run id, the number of input rows and the batch ids.
steps.observe: A query id stays the same across restarts from one checkpoint; the run id changes on each start.

steps.title: Reading results back as a sorted bag
steps.explanation: bag and validatedBag check the output schema, bound the size before collecting to the driver, and turn rows into id:cents strings sorted by id then cents. Sorting makes the comparison independent of file and partition order. The resume and replay helpers reuse runParquet with different inputs; separateReplay first proves that its checkpoint and output are new paths. guaranteeLedger returns row count, distinct ids and total cents.
steps.observe: Results are compared as sorted lists, so duplicates stay visible.

steps.excerpt:
def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    var ownedRoot: Path = null
    val spark = SparkSession
      .builder()
      .appName("ds60-spark-035")
      .master("local[2]")
      .config("spark.ui.enabled", "false")
      .config("spark.driver.host", "127.0.0.1")
      .config("spark.driver.bindAddress", "127.0.0.1")
      .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "2")
      .config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false")
      .config("spark.sql.ansi.enabled", "true")
      .config("spark.sql.session.timeZone", "UTC")
      .getOrCreate()
    try {
      require(spark.sparkContext.master == "local[2]", "local-only course session")
      spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR")
      require(spark.version == "4.3.0", "Prepared Spark 4.3.0 required")
      spark.conf.set("spark.sql.streaming.stopTimeout", "5000")
      ownedRoot = Files.createTempDirectory(Paths.get(".").toAbsolutePath.normalize(), "spark-035-")
      val input = ownedRoot.resolve("input"); val checkpoint = ownedRoot.resolve("checkpoint");
      val output = ownedRoot.resolve("output")
      publishFile(
        ownedRoot,
        input,
        "batch-01.json",
        Seq("""{"id":1,"cents":100}""", """{"id":2,"cents":200}""")
      )
      // Exercise 1: Validate the finite input and output grain
      val initial = spark.read.schema(eventSchema).json(input.toString)
      assert(validatedBag(initial) == Seq("1:100", "2:200"))
      var nullRejected = false
      try validatedBag(initial.withColumn("id", lit(null).cast("long")))
      catch { case _: IllegalArgumentException => nullRejected = true }
      assert(nullRejected)
steps.title: A pinned local session, the first file and an input check
steps.explanation: The session runs locally with fixed settings and requires Spark 4.3.0, so the lesson fails clearly on any other version. stopTimeout bounds how long stopping a query may take. The scratch root is created under the working directory, and the first file publishes ids 1 and 2. Before streaming anything, a static spark.read of the same folder is checked with validatedBag, and a copy whose id column is forced to null must be rejected with IllegalArgumentException.
steps.observe: The static read returns 1:100 and 2:200, and the null id copy is rejected.

      val first = firstRun(spark, input, checkpoint, output)
      assert(first.inputRows == 2L && first.batches.nonEmpty)
      assert(bag(spark, output) == Seq("1:100", "2:200"))
      assert(!ownedQueries.last.isActive)
      // Exercise 3: Resume the same checkpoint after a new file
      val second = resumeNewFile(spark, ownedRoot, input, checkpoint, output)
      assert(second.id == first.id && second.runId != first.runId && second.inputRows == 2L)
      assert(bag(spark, output) == Seq("1:100", "2:200", "2:200", "3:300"))
      // Exercise 4: Resume with no new source files
      val before = bag(spark, output)
      val empty = resumeEmpty(spark, input, checkpoint, output)
      assert(empty.id == first.id && empty.inputRows == 0L && bag(spark, output) == before)
steps.title: First run, resume after a new file, resume with nothing new
steps.explanation: The first run reads two rows and the query is no longer active afterwards. The second file repeats id 2 and adds id 3. Restarting from the same checkpoint keeps the same query id, gets a new run id, and reads only the new file, because the checkpoint remembers which files were already processed. The output now holds four rows, including a duplicate 2:200 that came from the data, not from reprocessing. A third start with no new files reads zero rows and leaves the output unchanged.
steps.observe: The output becomes 1:100, 2:200, 2:200, 3:300, and the empty resume reads 0 rows.

steps.title: Replay with a new checkpoint, then the ledger and cleanup
steps.explanation: A new checkpoint has no memory, so the replay query gets a new id and reads all four input rows again into its own output folder. Writing a replay into the original output would duplicate everything; keeping it separate preserves both. The ledger counts 4 rows, 3 distinct ids and 800 cents. The finally block stops any active query before deleting scratch, then stops the session even if cleanup fails.
steps.observe: The program prints a line that starts: spark-035: six Scala reference contracts passed; Spark=4.3.0
